Plus, it limits what she can and can't do; for example, if she decides another female politician is the best VP pick, she can't necessarily pick her because that may turn off voters (I saw a poll recently that indicated a significant percentage of voters would be "concerned" about voting for an all-woman ticket). It's also worth noting that women running for office often take a hit in favorability. People might not even mind voting for a woman in the abstract, but as soon as you apply names to it, things get murkier. It's easy to forget that women are still incredibly underrepresented in politics, and it was even worse in very recent memory, so there aren't very many high-ranking women to substitute in when people say "I'd vote for a woman other than her," which keeps the question in the hypothetical and out of the real world.

Wikipedia also has some good breakdowns on the subject of women in legislative bodies, as well as their page on governors, for those who want to look at all the usual places to look for potential presidential candidates. For some interesting breakdowns:

* Women didn't break 5% representation in the House until 1989. They hit 10% in 1993.

* They didn't do so in the Senate until 1993 and 2001.

* Also, 1992 was the first time a state had two women in the Senate concurrently. It has only happened four times since, and only three of those four were via both being elected (one was appointed and immediately lost re-election).

* For governors, it was 1987 for 5% (which, it's worth noting, is only 3) and 2001 for 10% (which is only 5).

* There have never been 10 female governors concurrently; they've had nine over two different periods combining for 418 days.

* 23 states have never elected a female governor. 23 have also never elected a female senator. Most shockingly, 6 haven't ever elected a female representative. 1 state has never elected a woman to any of the three.

* There have been almost as many different female senators (46) as there have been presidents overall (43).

* House representation is the highest it's ever been, but is only 19.4%. Same with the Senate, at 20%. There are also 6 female governors.

So yeah, for a long time, there just weren't many women getting elected to things. That makes high-ranking positions like Speaker (or President) hard to reach.
